extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; readers of literary criticism and literary history
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical principles for judging poets and their works (tone, invention, execution, moral effect, style, keeping, originality). Extracts Hazlitt's recurring standards for what makes poetic/prose writing successful or faulty, illustrated by examples (Gay, Swift, Rabelais, Voltaire, Collins, Gray, Goldsmith, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of feeling vs affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: True poetic feeling should arise from 'powerful impulse or real feeling' rather than from conscious artifice or a wish to supply natural feeling by 'labour and art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt criticises Prior's 'sentimental and romantic productions' as 'mere affectation' — a symptom of self-conscious deficiency. Prefer spontaneous, inwardly compelled emotion to clever workmanship that merely simulates feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial awareness and intentionality in tone
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's control and awareness of what he is about affects quality — inadvertent grossness (lack of awareness) is less culpable than systematic affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gay is 'sometimes grosser than Prior, not systematically, but inadvertently--from not being so well aware of what he was about.' Consciousness of tone and intention is a criterion when judging lapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of invention (inventiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount and fertility of invention displayed in a work is a mark of merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gay's Fables praised for the 'quantity of invention implied'; inventive richness is a positive dimension even when other faults exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance and facility of execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness, elegance, and apparent ease in execution are important qualities of poetic writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt lauds Gay's 'elegance and facility of the execution' as part of what makes the Fables meritorious; execution can redeem or enhance inventive material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy, concision, and avoidance of diffuseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Good poetic/prose pieces avoid being 'spun out too long'; descriptions and narrative should not be 'too diffuse and desultory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt faults Gay's Fables as 'spun out too long' with diffuse narrative and sometimes morals 'without point.' Concision and focus are expected virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and fitness of moral or thematic point
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work includes a moral or explicit point, it should be pointed and relevant rather than vague or pointless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt says Gay's moral is 'sometimes without point'; a clear, well-expressed moral/lesson is a positive criterion for fables and didactic pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriateness and keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should respect or coherently transform its genre; 'keeping' and a sense of proper manner are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt notes some of Gay's pieces are 'more like Tales than Fables.' He praises works that maintain 'perfect keeping' (Swift's Gulliver's Travels) and criticises pieces that misalign with their stated form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to elevate coarse material (alchemy of mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: A high merit is the ability to extract refinement and grace from vulgar or coarse materials — turning 'dross into gold.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt calls the Beggar's Opera a triumph where 'the elegance of the composition is in exact proportion to the coarseness of the materials' — skillfully converting low life into refined art without losing truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of probability and naturalness
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when stylizing or employing licence, a writer should not 'violate probability' or 'o'erstep the modesty of nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Gay for effecting transformation 'without once violating probability.' Maintaining plausibility and natural behaviour is a yardstick of good art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of voice and naiveté in character
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' language and emotional expression should be appropriate to their social position and temperament — simplicity and 'naivete' are virtues when fitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt cites Polly's song as having 'touching simplicity' and 'characteristic propriety and naivete' — matching voice to character enhances verisimilitude and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to character and costume (local colour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete preservation of character, costume, and local detail grounds a work and lends truth to its portrayals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Gay: 'The preservation of the character and costume is complete.' Authentic detail and social costume are markers of skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtlety and depth of the general view of human life
rubrics_metrics.description: A superior work presents a subtle, abstracted, and penetrating view of human life and moral conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt admires Gay's 'general view ... of the most subtle and abstracted kind' and the detection of disguises rank lends to vice — depth of moral vision is a criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced use of wit and satire (tempering offensiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and sarcasm should be deployed so as to sharpen satire without making it gratuitously offensive; wit can mellow satire's harshness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt notes 'Every line ... sparkles with wit' and that 'the very wit ... takes off from the offensiveness of the satire.' Effective satire balances sting and charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral insight and universality (showing vulgarity of vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work should convincingly show moral truths, e.g., the commonality of vice across classes, in ways that illuminate human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt interprets the moral of Beggar's Opera 'to shew the vulgarity of vice' — moral generalisations that reveal universal truths are valued when convincingly argued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive formal adaptation for character (form suited to voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventing or adapting stanza/form to suit particular speakers or characters (e.g., creating new stanza types) is a mark of technical resourcefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Swift's invention of new stanza forms for character-voices (Mary the cookmaid), showing appropriate technical choices to serve dramatic or comic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tonal range and mixture (irony, pathos, whimsy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality may rest on a poet's or prose writer's ability to combine dry humour, irony, touching pathos, whimsy, and eccentric pleasantry in harmonious proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt attributes Swift's strength to a mix of 'dry humour, an exquisite tone of irony, touching, unpretending pathos' — tonal complexity is prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception versus execution (power of invention and craftsmanship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence may lie in conception (invention) or execution (craft); the presence of power — whether in idea or execution — is the ultimate test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On Gulliver's Travels Hazlitt argues the power may be in conception or execution but 'the power is somewhere' — both conception and workmanship count; criticizing mechanical execution as diminishing value is misguided when the underlying power is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision, presence of mind, and 'keeping' in sustained conceit
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended conceits or imaginative premises should be handled with 'mathematical precision' and sustained 'keeping' to succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Swift's reduction of things to scales (Lilliput/Brobdingnag) as executed 'with mathematical precision, with complete presence of mind and perfect keeping.' Controlled execution of bold conceits is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral seriousness and incisive perception as source of ludicrous effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The ludicrous often arises from a keen moral sense of impropriety; wit that separates truth from falsehood with 'force, precision, and honest abruptness' is effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt explains Swift's ludicrousness springs from 'keen sense of impropriety' and a talent for sharp moral separation — moral perception fuels effective ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of light/trifling pieces as relaxation
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional trivial or playful pieces are acceptable and can function as relaxation from an author's habitual seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt defends Swift's 'lack-a-daisical, slip-shod, tedious, trifling' verses as proofs of readiness to oblige and as respite ('a relaxation from the excessive earnestness').

rubrics_metrics.name: Exuberant vitality and lexical richness (Rabelaisian quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer may be judged by exuberance of enjoyment, lavishness of invention and a language 'of marrow' — generous, unctuous diction and prodigious style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt describes Rabelais as luxuriating in nonsense, with a prodigious style; such exuberance and wealth of words are positive when appropriate to temperament and aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy, subtlety, and delicate tact (Voltairean quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtle indirectness, concise expression, and 'sang-froid' that inflicts wounds indistinctly but effectively are valued modes of satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Voltaire's 'delicacy of tact,' 'indirect hints,' and few-word blows; economy and refined irony are distinct virtues from boisterous exuberance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and tautness of style (every sentence telling)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work in which 'every sentence tells' and which reads with unity and cohesion (even to the effect of 'the whole reads like one sentence') is exemplary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt cites Candide: 'Every sentence tells, and the whole reads like one sentence.' Tight, cohesive style and economy are praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in moralising; avoid overloading reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral reflection should be powerful but not overloaded with excessive horror or scholastic verbosity that oppresses attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt criticises Young for overloading excellent moral reflections 'with a religious horror' and 'perpetual and violent demands upon' the reader; moderation and felicitous expression are preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivida vis, lasting impression and genuine inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should leave lasting 'stings' or traces of thought and feeling in readers' minds — evidence of 'vivida vis' or genuine inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Collins for lines that 'leave stings in the minds of his readers' — enduring emotional resonance is a key criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attic simplicity, pathos, and fervour of imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'attic simplicity' and sincere pathos combined with fervent imagination constitute high poetic virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt selects Collins' best works for their 'attic simplicity, a pathos, and fervour of imagination' — simplicity allied to depth is ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from affectation in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose merits include natural, unpretentious expression; prose that 'pours his thoughts out ... without pretence' is praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt lauds Gray's prose as 'quite free from affectation' — unforced, candid prose is a virtue distinct from poetic ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity vs performance (avoid courting admiration by affectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer who affects traits (privacy, modesty) for popularity is censured; sincerity of temperament is a criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt criticises Shenstone for 'affecting privacy' to be admired — authentic disposition preferred over artful posing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pruning redundances; revision as improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing away redundancy and excessive ornament improves poetic works; later pruning can enhance effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt notes Akenside 'improved ... by pruning away a great many redundances of style and ornament' — revision and restraint are technical virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of tone to subject (coarseness or strength when deserved)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone should fit subject matter; strong, coarse satire may be appropriate for certain targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt allows Churchill's 'strong, coarse' satires as fitting their subjects — judge tone by aptness rather than by uniform propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowing elegance and felicitous turns of phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluency and elegant versification, together with felicitous phrasing (repeated to good effect), are marks of distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Goldsmith as 'the most flowing and elegant of our versifiers since Pope' with 'peculiar felicity in his turns upon words.' Smooth melodic diction is prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of originality and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may combine imitation of models with original embellishment; both capacities (drawing on models and adorning them) can be virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt observes Goldsmith 'could do nothing without some model before him, and he could copy nothing that he did not adorn' — successful adaptation and tasteful borrowing are positive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to charm across genres (comic, novelistic, didactic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary artist's ability to succeed in multiple modes (comic writer, novelist, essayist) and to charm wide audiences is a mark of eminence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt notes Goldsmith's success as novelist (Vicar of Wakefield), comic dramatist (Tony Lumpkin), and essayist (Citizen of the World) — versatility and consistent charm count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity advantage in certain forms (sonnet virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short forms (sonnets) have advantages; brevity can help treat pleasing subjects in a philosophical, concentrated way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Warton's sonnets and remarks that the sonnet 'has the necessary advantage of being short' though it can be 'tedious and brief' if mishandled.
